lesson.subtitle: Lesson 16 -- Checkpoint: Five Minutes on Your Own Work
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Liliane Meira | Lesson 16 -- Checkpoint: Five Minutes on Your Own Work

listenings.text: Five minutes feels short until you are the one speaking. The people who do it well have a plan, and they let the listener see it. They signpost: first I will tell you what I make, then how it started, and then where it is going. They pace themselves, so the first minute is not a race. And they are not afraid of silence. A pause is much better than a filler. Um, you know, like, sort of: every filler tells the audience that you are still searching. If you stumble over a word, do not apologize. Just say it again, slowly, and continue. Nobody remembers a stumble. People remember the one sentence you said clearly. And in the last thirty seconds, wrap up. Go back to the first idea, say it in a new way, and stop. Ending on time is a kind of respect.

Every few months I ask my students to record the same task again: five minutes about their own work. Then we listen to the first recording and the new one, side by side. That is the benchmark, and it is much more honest than a test. At B2, progress is rarely a single breakthrough. It is quieter than that. The sentences get longer. The pauses move: they stop happening in the middle of a phrase and start happening between ideas. The speaker holds back less, and builds on what was said a minute earlier instead of starting again. What I ask my students to notice is not how many mistakes they made, but which mistakes have disappeared. When you look back on two recordings, that is the real measure of a block of lessons.
